title: How the Web Works: Client-Server, DNS, HTTP
summary: Every design starts with a client sending a request to a server. Interviewers expect you to narrate the request path (DNS, TCP/TLS, HTTP) without hand-waving.

resources.label: What happens when you type a URL into your browser?

questions: Walk through every hop from typing a URL to seeing the page.
What do the recursive resolver, root, TLD, and authoritative nameservers each do?
Why is HTTP called stateless, and how do apps keep sessions anyway?
What does TLS add on top of TCP, and what does it cost in latency?
exercise: Sketch the full request path for loading a web app you use every day: browser cache, DNS lookup, TCP + TLS handshake, HTTP request, server, database, response. Mark which steps are cached and roughly how many ms each takes.

title: Latency vs Throughput, Performance vs Scalability
summary: The vocabulary interviewers use to judge trade-offs. You need to state what you are optimizing for (latency, throughput, availability) before choosing components.

resources.label: Performance vs scalability, Latency vs throughput, Availability in numbers

questions: Define latency and throughput. Give an example where improving one hurts the other.
What is the difference between a performance problem and a scalability problem?
What does 99.9% vs 99.99% availability mean in downtime per year?
Roughly how long is a memory read vs SSD read vs cross-continent round trip?
exercise: A rocket test-stand data acquisition (DAQ) system samples 8 channels at 10 kHz and streams to a laptop. Write down its latency budget and required throughput (bytes/s), then list two changes that improve throughput but worsen latency (e.g., batching).

title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
summary: Scaling up a single box hits a ceiling; scaling out needs stateless servers and shared state elsewhere. This is the backbone of almost every interview answer.

resources.label: Scale From Zero To Millions Of Users (book chapter)
Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling: Key Differences

questions: When is vertical scaling the right call, and what are its limits?
Why must web servers be stateless to scale horizontally? Where does session state go?
What new problems appear once you have more than one server?
In what order would you add components as traffic grows 10x, 100x, 1000x?
exercise: Draw your web app at 3 stages: 100 users (one box), 100k users, 10M users. For each stage, list exactly what you added (LB, replicas, cache, CDN, stateless tier) and why.

title: Load Balancers & Reverse Proxies
summary: Load balancers spread traffic and hide failed servers. Interviewers want to hear L4 vs L7, the algorithm you'd pick, and how health checks work.

resources.label: What is a LOAD BALANCER really about?

questions: What is the difference between L4 and L7 load balancing?
Compare round robin, least connections, and IP/consistent hashing. When does each fit?
How do health checks and failover work? What if the load balancer itself dies?
How is a reverse proxy different from a load balancer?
exercise: You have 4 app servers, one of which is 2x as powerful, and WebSocket clients that must stay on one server. Pick an algorithm, explain sticky sessions vs hashing, and draw an active-passive LB pair.

title: Caching: Strategies, Eviction, Invalidation
summary: Caching is the most common answer to 'make reads faster'. You must know where caches live and the consistency cost of each write strategy.

resources.label: Cache Systems Every Developer Should Know
When to update the cache (cache-aside, write-through, write-behind)

questions: List the layers where a cache can live, from browser to database.
Compare cache-aside, write-through, and write-back. Which risks data loss?
Explain LRU vs LFU eviction and what TTLs are for.
What are cache stampede and hot keys, and how do you mitigate them?
exercise: Design caching for a profile page read 1000x more than it's written. Choose a strategy, TTL, and eviction policy; then describe exactly what happens on a profile update so readers never see stale data for more than 5 seconds.

title: SQL vs NoSQL & Data Modeling
summary: Picking a database and sketching a schema is a step in every interview. Interviewers want a justified choice tied to access patterns, not a buzzword.

resources.label: How To Choose The Right Database?

questions: What does ACID give you, and which workloads need it?
Name the four NoSQL families and a use case for each.
When do you normalize vs denormalize?
How do access patterns drive the choice of primary key in a key-value or wide-column store?
exercise: Model a Ticketmaster-lite: users, events, seats, bookings. Write the SQL tables with keys, then rewrite the 'get my bookings' and 'get seats for event' access patterns for a key-value store and note what you lost.

title: Week 1 Review: From One Server to Many
summary: Recap the request path, scaling, load balancing, caching, and database choice. Practice combining them into one coherent diagram.

resources.label: 8 Most Important System Design Concepts You Should Know

questions: Explain, start to finish, how a request reaches your database in a horizontally scaled app.
Which component would you add first for a read-heavy app, and why?
What is the consistency cost of adding a cache?
SQL or NoSQL for a user-accounts table? Defend it in 30 seconds.
exercise: Design on paper: a college club event-signup site that gets a 50x spike when registration opens. Draw DNS, CDN, LB, stateless app servers, cache, and DB. Label what's cached, the eviction policy, and what happens when one app server dies mid-spike.

title: Database Indexing
summary: Indexes turn full table scans into fast lookups, at the cost of slower writes. Interviewers expect you to name the index that supports each query.

resources.label: DB Indexing in System Design Interviews (B-tree, Geospatial, Inverted Index)

questions: How does a B-tree index make lookups O(log n)?
Why do indexes slow down writes and use more storage?
What is a composite index, and why does column order matter?
When would you use a hash, inverted, or geospatial index instead of a B-tree?
exercise: For a messages table (id, chat_id, sender_id, created_at, body), write the indexes you'd create for: 'latest 50 messages in a chat', 'all messages by a user', and 'search message text'. Justify each and note which one doesn't belong in Postgres.

title: Replication
summary: Replication copies data to multiple machines for availability and read scaling. Interviewers probe leader-follower trade-offs and replication lag.

resources.label: Distributed Consensus and Data Replication Strategies

questions: Compare leader-follower, multi-leader, and leaderless replication.
What is replication lag, and what user-visible bug can it cause?
Synchronous vs asynchronous replication: what do you trade?
What happens during failover, and what is split-brain?
exercise: Your app uses 1 leader + 2 async read replicas. A user updates their bio and immediately reloads and sees the old bio. Explain why, then give two fixes (e.g., read-your-writes routing) and their costs.

title: Sharding & Partitioning
summary: When one database can't hold the data or the writes, you split it. Choosing a shard key is a favorite interview deep dive.

resources.label: A Crash Course on Database Sharding

questions: Range vs hash vs directory-based sharding: pros and cons of each?
What makes a good shard key? Give a bad one and explain the hotspot.
How do you handle queries or joins that span shards?
Sharding vs replication: what does each solve? Do you need both?
exercise: Shard a chat app's messages table (1B messages/day). Compare shard keys user_id, chat_id, and message_id for the query 'load a chat's recent messages'. Pick one, then explain what happens when a celebrity group chat becomes a hotspot.

title: Consistent Hashing
summary: Consistent hashing lets you add or remove nodes while moving only a small fraction of keys. It underpins caches, Dynamo-style stores, and load balancers.

resources.label: Consistent Hashing | Algorithms You Should Know #1

questions: Why does hash(key) % N break when N changes?
Walk through placing servers and keys on a hash ring.
What problem do virtual nodes solve?
Name two real systems that use consistent hashing.
exercise: Draw a ring with 3 cache nodes and 8 keys. Add a 4th node and mark which keys move. Then add virtual nodes (3 per server) and explain how load evens out.

title: CAP Theorem & Consistency Models
summary: During a network partition you must choose consistency or availability. Interviewers want you to pick per feature (e.g., bookings vs likes) and say why.
questions: State CAP precisely. Why is 'pick 2 of 3' misleading?
Strong vs eventual consistency: give a feature that needs each.
What is read-your-writes or causal consistency, and when is it enough?
Is a ticket-booking system CP or AP? A social feed?
exercise: For a drone fleet app, classify each feature as needing strong or eventual consistency: mission assignment, battery telemetry display, geofence updates, flight log archive. Justify each in one sentence and note what the user sees during a partition.

title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
summary: Quick math (QPS, storage, bandwidth) justifies your design choices. Interviewers watch for sane orders of magnitude, not precision.

resources.label: Powers of two table + Latency numbers

questions: How many seconds are in a day (roughly), and how do you turn DAU into QPS?
How do you estimate peak QPS from average QPS?
Estimate 5 years of storage for 10M daily 1 KB writes.
When does an estimate change your design (e.g., 'fits in one machine's memory')?
exercise: Estimate for a Twitter-like app with 50M DAU, 2 posts/user/day, 100 feed reads/user/day, 1 KB posts and 10% with a 500 KB image: write QPS, read QPS, peak QPS, daily and 5-year storage, and egress bandwidth. Show your rounding.

title: Week 2 Review: Data at Scale
summary: Recap indexing, replication, sharding, consistent hashing, CAP, and estimation, the toolkit for any data-heavy deep dive.

resources.label: 7 Must-know Strategies to Scale Your Database
CAP Theorem in System Design Interviews

questions: When do you add an index vs a read replica vs a shard?
Explain how consistent hashing and replication work together in a Dynamo-style store.
What consistency does a user get reading from an async replica?
Estimate: does 2 TB of data fit on one database node? Should it?
exercise: Design on paper: a rocket team's test-run database (Postgres) has grown to 2 TB with 5k reads/s and 200 writes/s. Estimate 1-year growth, then propose indexes, read replicas, and a shard key. Explain where consistent hashing would (or wouldn't) help.

title: Message Queues & Pub/Sub
summary: Queues decouple producers from consumers and absorb bursts. Interviewers expect you to know queue vs pub/sub vs log (Kafka) and delivery guarantees.
questions: What is the difference between a point-to-point queue and pub/sub?
At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once: what does each mean in practice?
How does a Kafka topic/partition/consumer-group model work?
Why must consumers often be idempotent?
exercise: Your test stand produces sensor packets, and three consumers need them: a live dashboard, a disk archiver, and an anomaly detector. Draw it with a queue vs with pub/sub (or a Kafka topic). Which delivery guarantee does each consumer need?

title: Async Processing & Background Jobs
summary: Slow work (emails, video encoding, reports) belongs off the request path. Interviewers look for queues, workers, retries, and back pressure.

resources.label: Asynchronism: message queues, task queues, back pressure
Message Queues in System Design Interviews

questions: Which work should be synchronous vs asynchronous in a signup flow?
How do workers retry safely, and when does a message go to a dead-letter queue?
What is back pressure, and what happens without it?
How do you report job status back to the user?
exercise: Design 'upload a CSV of 1M rows and import it': the API returns immediately with a job ID, workers process chunks, and the client polls for progress. Show the queue, worker pool, retry policy, DLQ, and the status table.

title: API Design: REST, gRPC, WebSockets, Pagination, Idempotency
summary: Defining the API is an explicit interview step. You need to pick a protocol, design clean endpoints, paginate, and make retries safe.

resources.label: Top 6 Most Popular API Architecture Styles
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

questions: When would you choose REST vs gRPC vs WebSockets (or SSE)?
Offset vs cursor pagination: why does cursor pagination scale better?
Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and how do idempotency keys make POST safe to retry?
How do you version an API?
exercise: Write the API for a drone mission-control app: list drones (paginated), assign a mission (idempotent), and stream live telemetry. Give method, path, request/response shape, and protocol for each.

title: Rate Limiting
summary: Rate limiters protect services from abuse and overload. Expect questions on algorithms and where the limiter lives in a distributed system.

resources.label: Scaling your API with rate limiters
Rate Limiter System Design: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Scaling

questions: Compare token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, and sliding window.
Where can a rate limiter live (client, gateway, service), and what are the trade-offs?
How do you rate limit consistently across many servers?
What should the API return when a client is limited?
exercise: Implement token bucket in pseudocode (capacity 10, refill 1/sec) and trace 15 requests arriving in 2 seconds. Then explain how you'd share bucket state across 20 API servers.

title: Blob Storage & CDNs
summary: Images, video, and logs go in object storage, not your database, and get served through a CDN. Presigned URLs are a common interview detail.

resources.label: Object Storage in System Design Interviews

questions: Why not store large files in a relational database?
How do presigned URLs let clients upload directly to blob storage?
Push vs pull CDN: how does each get content to the edge?
How do you upload a 5 GB file reliably (multipart, resumable)?
exercise: Design profile-photo upload: client asks the API for a presigned URL, uploads to object storage, a thumbnail job runs, and the photo is served via CDN. Draw it and list what metadata lives in the database.

title: Monitoring & Observability
summary: You can't run what you can't see. Interviewers like candidates who mention metrics, logs, traces, and alerting on the golden signals.
questions: What are the four golden signals?
Metrics vs logs vs traces: what question does each answer?
What makes a good alert vs a noisy one?
What are SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs?
exercise: For a telemetry ingestion service, define 2 SLIs and SLOs, 4 dashboard metrics, and 2 pages-worthy alerts. Then describe how a trace would show you a slow database call.

title: Week 3 Review: Async Systems & APIs
summary: Recap queues, async jobs, API design, rate limiting, blob storage, and observability, the building blocks that show up in every design problem.
questions: When do you reach for a queue vs a synchronous call?
How do idempotency keys and at-least-once delivery fit together?
Where would you put a rate limiter in a public API?
What 3 metrics would you alert on for any web service?
exercise: Design on paper: an image-upload + thumbnail service. Include the upload API (presigned URLs), a queue for thumbnail jobs with retries/DLQ, blob storage + CDN, a per-user rate limit, and three alerts.

title: The System Design Interview Framework
summary: A repeatable 45-minute structure: requirements, estimation, core entities, API, high-level design, deep dives. Using it is half of what interviewers grade.

resources.label: System Design Interview: A Step-By-Step Guide
A Framework For System Design Interviews (book chapter)

questions: What are the steps of the framework, and roughly how many minutes go to each?
Functional vs non-functional requirements: give two of each for a chat app.
When should you skip or shorten estimation?
How do you choose what to deep-dive on?
exercise: Take 'Design Spotify playlists' and do only the first 10 minutes of the framework: 3 functional requirements, 3 non-functional, core entities, and the API. Time yourself.

title: Design a URL Shortener (Bitly)
summary: The classic warm-up: short-code generation, a read-heavy redirect path, and caching. Tests the basics of the framework end to end.

resources.label: Design a URL Shortener Like Bitly
How Does a URL Shortener Work?

questions: How do you generate unique short codes (hash vs counter + base62)? What about collisions?
301 vs 302 redirect: which and why?
What is the read:write ratio, and how does it shape the design?
How do you support custom aliases and expiration?
exercise: Design Bitly: write requirements, estimate QPS/storage for 100M new URLs/month, define the API and data model, draw the high-level design, then deep-dive on short-code generation at scale.

title: Design Pastebin
summary: Like Bitly but with large text blobs, which forces you to separate metadata (DB) from content (object storage).
questions: Where do paste contents live vs paste metadata, and why?
How do you expire pastes efficiently?
How would you track view analytics without slowing reads?
How does a CDN help for popular pastes?
exercise: Design Pastebin: requirements (create, read, expire), estimate storage for 10M pastes/day at 10 KB, API, data model, high-level design, then deep-dive on expiration cleanup and caching hot pastes.

title: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter
summary: Turns day 18's algorithms into a full design: shared counters, low latency, and failure behavior across many servers.

resources.label: Design A Rate Limiter (book chapter, skim Step 3)

questions: Where does the rate limiter sit in the request path?
How do you make counter updates atomic in Redis?
Should the limiter fail open or fail closed if Redis is down?
How do you configure different limits per user tier or endpoint?
exercise: Design a rate limiter for an API gateway serving 1M req/s: requirements, estimate Redis memory for 10M users, choose an algorithm, draw the design, then deep-dive on race conditions and multi-region limits.

title: Design a Distributed Unique ID Generator
summary: Many designs need globally unique, roughly sortable IDs without a single bottleneck. Snowflake-style IDs are the standard answer.
questions: Why not use auto-increment or UUIDv4 everywhere?
Break down the bits of a Snowflake ID.
What happens if a machine's clock moves backward?
How are worker IDs assigned without collisions?
exercise: Design an ID service producing 100k IDs/s across 3 data centers: requirements, bit layout, API, worker-ID assignment, then deep-dive on clock skew and what your code does when NTP jumps the clock back.

title: Design a Key-Value Store
summary: Combines partitioning, replication, consistency, and failure detection into one system (think DynamoDB/Cassandra).

resources.label: How Key-value Stores Work (Redis, DynamoDB, Memcached)

questions: How do consistent hashing and replication combine to place data?
Explain quorum reads/writes (N, R, W). What does R + W > N guarantee?
How are conflicts resolved (vector clocks, last-write-wins)?
How do nodes detect failures (gossip, hinted handoff)?
exercise: Design a key-value store with get/put: requirements (high availability, tunable consistency), estimate for 10 TB, API, partitioning + replication scheme, then deep-dive on N/R/W choices and handling a node that is down for 1 hour.

title: Week 4 Review: Framework & First Designs
summary: Recap the framework and the first five problems: URL shortener, Pastebin, rate limiter, ID generator, key-value store.

resources.label: How to Prepare for System Design Interviews
Consistent Hashing: Easy Explanation for System Design Interviews
How to approach a system design interview question

questions: Recite the framework steps and time budget from memory.
How does Pastebin's design differ from Bitly's, and why?
Where did consistent hashing show up this week?
What's your default answer for 'make it highly available'?
exercise: Design on paper in 20 minutes using the full framework: a 'link-in-bio' page service (users create a page of links; visitors view it; owners see click counts). Time each step and note where you ran over.

title: Design a News Feed
summary: The fan-out problem: precompute feeds on write or assemble them on read? A core interview question about read/write trade-offs.

resources.label: Design A News Feed System (book chapter)

questions: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read: trade-offs?
How do you handle celebrities with 10M followers?
How do you paginate a feed that keeps changing?
What goes in the feed cache, and how big is it?
exercise: Design a news feed for 500M DAU: requirements, estimate feed reads/s and fan-out writes/s, API, data model (posts, follows, feed cache), high-level design, then deep-dive on the hybrid fan-out strategy for celebrities.

title: Design a Chat App (WhatsApp)
summary: Real-time messaging over persistent connections, with delivery guarantees, ordering, and offline users.

resources.label: Design a Messaging App Like WhatsApp
Design A Chat System (WhatsApp, Messenger, Discord, Slack)

questions: Why WebSockets instead of HTTP polling for chat?
How do you route a message to a user connected to a different server?
How do you deliver messages to offline users and sync multiple devices?
How do you guarantee per-chat message ordering?
exercise: Design WhatsApp 1:1 and group chat: requirements, estimate concurrent connections and messages/s for 100M DAU, API/events, data model, high-level design, then deep-dive on routing between chat servers (pub/sub) and offline delivery.

title: Design a Notification System
summary: One service that fans out push, SMS, and email reliably, with user preferences, retries, and rate limits per channel.

resources.label: Notification Service | Systems Design Interview Questions

questions: How do you decouple producers from push/SMS/email senders?
How do you avoid sending duplicate notifications on retries?
Where do user preferences and opt-outs get checked?
How do you handle a third-party provider (APNs/Twilio) outage?
exercise: Design a notification service for 10M users: requirements, estimate notifications/s at peak, API, data model (templates, preferences, delivery log), high-level design with per-channel queues, then deep-dive on dedup and retries.

title: Design a Web Crawler
summary: A distributed pipeline problem: URL frontier, politeness, dedup, and fault tolerance at billions of pages.

resources.label: Design A Web Crawler (book chapter, skim)

questions: What is the URL frontier, and how do you enforce politeness per domain?
How do you detect duplicate URLs and duplicate content?
How do you recover if a crawler worker dies mid-crawl?
How would you estimate time to crawl 1B pages?
exercise: Design a crawler for 1B pages in 5 days: requirements, estimate pages/s and storage, components (frontier, fetchers, parser, dedup, storage), high-level design, then deep-dive on politeness and DNS caching.

title: Design Search Autocomplete
summary: Return the top suggestions for a prefix in under 100 ms. Tests data structures (tries) plus an offline aggregation pipeline.

resources.label: Design Autocomplete or Typeahead Suggestions for Google Search

questions: How does a trie with cached top-k at each node answer a prefix query fast?
How are query frequencies collected and the trie rebuilt?
How do you shard the trie?
Where do client-side debouncing and caching help?
exercise: Design autocomplete for 10M DAU: requirements (top 5, <100 ms), estimate queries/s, API, data structures, high-level design (query service + offline aggregation), then deep-dive on updating suggestions without downtime.

title: Design Ticketmaster
summary: High-contention booking: thousands of users fighting for the same seats. Tests transactions, locking, and surge handling.

resources.label: Design a Ticket Booking Site Like Ticketmaster
ACID Properties in Databases With Examples

questions: How do you prevent two users from booking the same seat?
Pessimistic locking vs optimistic concurrency vs a reservation TTL?
How do you handle 1M users hitting a popular on-sale at once (virtual queue)?
Which parts need strong consistency, and which can be eventually consistent?
exercise: Design Ticketmaster: requirements (view events, reserve, pay), estimate peak QPS for a huge on-sale, API, data model, high-level design, then deep-dive on seat reservation with a 10-minute hold and the waiting-room queue.

title: Week 5 Review: Real-Time & Contention
summary: Recap news feed, chat, notifications, crawler, autocomplete, and Ticketmaster. Look for the repeated patterns across them.

resources.label: How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages

questions: Which designs this week used fan-out, and how did they differ?
Where did you need strong consistency, and how did you get it?
How do WebSocket servers find each other's users?
What did Discord change in its storage layer, and why?
exercise: Design on paper: @mention notifications in a group chat. A user mentioned in a 50k-member channel should get a push within 5 s. Reuse chat routing, notification fan-out, and dedup; draw it and identify the bottleneck.

title: Design Uber / Ride-Sharing
summary: Match riders to nearby drivers in real time. Tests geospatial indexing, high-frequency location updates, and consistency in matching.

resources.label: Design a Ride-Sharing Service Like Uber
H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index

questions: How do you store and query 'drivers within 2 km' efficiently?
How do you handle millions of location updates per second?
How do you ensure a driver isn't matched to two riders at once?
Geohash vs quadtree vs H3: trade-offs?
exercise: Design Uber: requirements (request ride, match, track), estimate location-update QPS for 1M active drivers, API, data model, high-level design, then deep-dive on the geospatial index and the matching lock.

title: Design Dropbox / File Sync
summary: Upload, store, and sync large files across devices. Tests blob storage, chunking, and change notifications.

resources.label: Design a File Storage Service Like Dropbox

questions: Why chunk files, and how does chunking enable resumable uploads and dedup?
How does a client learn another device changed a file?
Where do file metadata and file bytes live?
How do you handle conflicting edits from two offline devices?
exercise: Design Dropbox: requirements (upload, download, sync, share), estimate storage for 50M users, API, data model (files, chunks, versions), high-level design, then deep-dive on chunked uploads with presigned URLs and sync notifications.

title: Design YouTube / Video Streaming
summary: Upload, transcode, and stream video globally. Tests async pipelines, blob storage, CDNs, and adaptive bitrate streaming.

resources.label: Design a Video Streaming Platform Like YouTube

questions: What happens between upload and 'video is watchable'?
What is adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH), and why segment videos?
How do CDNs reduce origin load, and what about long-tail videos?
How do you support resumable uploads of a 10 GB file?
exercise: Design YouTube: requirements (upload, watch), estimate daily upload storage and egress bandwidth, API, data model, high-level design, then deep-dive on the transcoding pipeline (DAG of jobs) and CDN strategy.

title: Design a Distributed Job Scheduler
summary: Run millions of scheduled or delayed jobs reliably (cron at scale). Tests at-least-once execution, leasing, and idempotency.

resources.label: Executing Cron Scripts Reliably at Scale
How we designed Dropbox ATF: an async task framework

questions: How do you find jobs that are due without scanning the whole table?
How do you make sure a job runs once even if a worker crashes mid-run?
What is a lease/visibility timeout?
How do you scale the scheduler itself without double-scheduling?
exercise: Design a job scheduler supporting one-off and cron jobs (10k jobs/s due at peak): requirements, API, data model (jobs, executions), high-level design (scheduler, queue, workers), then deep-dive on exactly-once-ish execution with leases + idempotency.

title: Design Live Comments
summary: Push new comments to millions of viewers of a live video in real time. A deep dive on SSE/WebSockets and pub/sub fan-out.
questions: Polling vs long polling vs SSE vs WebSockets for this feature?
How do comments reach viewers connected to hundreds of different servers?
How do you load older comments when a viewer joins late?
How would you partition pub/sub channels for a video with 5M viewers?
exercise: Design live comments: requirements, estimate comments/s and fan-out messages/s, API, data model, high-level design, then deep-dive on routing comments to the right SSE servers via pub/sub.

title: Design Real-Time Drone Fleet Telemetry Ingestion + Dashboard
summary: Defense-flavored: ingest high-rate telemetry from thousands of drones over flaky links, store it, and show a live operator dashboard. Mirrors real Anduril/Shield AI work.

resources.label: Apache Kafka Fundamentals You Should Know

questions: Which protocol would drones use to send telemetry, and what QoS level?
How do you buffer on the drone and backfill after a link drop?
How do you store 10 Hz x 50 fields x 5,000 drones, and downsample for history?
How does the dashboard get live updates without hammering the database?
exercise: Design fleet telemetry for 5,000 drones at 10 Hz: requirements (live map, alerts, 1-year history), estimate msgs/s and storage/day, protocol + API, data model, high-level design (gateway, Kafka, stream processor, TSDB, WebSocket push), then deep-dive on handling a drone that reconnects with 10 minutes of buffered data.

title: Week 6 Review: Media, Geo & Streams
summary: Recap Uber, Dropbox, YouTube, job scheduler, live comments, and drone telemetry. Redis showed up repeatedly, so review it as a key technology.

resources.label: What Is Redis Really About? Why Is It So Popular?

questions: Name 4 Redis data structures and a design from this week that used each.
How did blob storage + CDN appear in both Dropbox and YouTube?
Compare how Uber and drone telemetry handle high-frequency location updates.
What makes a job scheduler different from a plain message queue?
exercise: Design on paper: 'Find My Squad', live location sharing for a 20-person team on a field exercise with spotty LTE. Reuse geo-indexing, WebSocket/SSE push, and edge buffering; draw it and name your consistency choice.

title: Design Top-K (Trending Videos)
summary: Compute the most-viewed items over sliding time windows at massive scale. Tests stream aggregation and approximate algorithms.

resources.label: Design YouTube's Top K Videos Feature
Algorithms You Should Know Before System Design Interviews

questions: Exact counting vs approximate (count-min sketch): when is approximate OK?
How do you compute top-k for last hour vs last day vs all time?
How do you merge partial top-k results from many partitions?
How fresh do results need to be, and how does that change the design?
exercise: Design trending top-100 videos for 1M view events/s: requirements, estimate, API, data model, high-level design (stream ingest, windowed counts, heap merge), then deep-dive on sliding windows.

title: Design an Ad Click Aggregator
summary: Count clicks accurately in near real time for billing and dashboards. A classic stream-processing design with exactly-once concerns.
questions: How do you count clicks without double counting on retries?
Lambda vs Kappa architecture: what's the difference?
How do you handle late-arriving events in windowed aggregation?
How do you reconcile the real-time count with a batch recount?
exercise: Design an ad click aggregator for 10k clicks/s: requirements (dashboard per minute, accurate billing), estimate, API, data model, high-level design (click service, Kafka, stream processor, OLAP store), then deep-dive on idempotent counting and reconciliation.

title: Design a Sensor Data Pipeline for a Test Stand
